documentation.range: This cobra is widely distributed in South Asia, occurring in Pakistan, India (where it is widespread throughout most of the country, incl. Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, [Dino Aulakh pers. comm.], Maharashtra, Kerala, Gujarat), Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, and Sri Lanka (Daniel 2002). It is found at elevations between 100 and 2,000 m asl. It is not known to occur west of Duki in Pakistan. While it has been suggested that it may occur in the Kabul River Valley in eastern Afghanistan (Wüster 1998, Sindaco et al. 2013) these records are likely to refer to Naja oxiana, which was previously considered a subspecies of N. naja and which is known to occur in Kabul Province (Wagner et al. 2016). Consequently Wagner et al. (2016) recommend that N. naja be removed from the Afghan herpetofauna. A record from Phong Nha - Ke Bang National Park in Viet Nam is presumed to represent a different species formerly included within N. naja, but the precise identity of this record is unclear (Ziegler et al. 2004)
documentation.population: This is a common species. Its population is thought to be stable across its range as a whole.
documentation.habitats: The Indian cobra is a highly adaptable species and is found in a wide variety of habitats ranging from moist evergreen forests, tropical dry deciduous forests, grassland habitat and dry scrub jungle to rice paddies. It is also found in artificial habitats and other agricultural lands. They can also be found near human habitations. They are diurnal snakes (though often seen in late evening hours) and take shelter in granaries, degraded termite mounds, earth dams, rock piles during the day. Indian cobras are oviparous and lay their eggs between the months of April and July. Females lay from 12 to 50 eggs underground in burrows and the eggs hatch 48 to 69 days later.   The young disperse one or two weeks thereafter. They lay eggs more than once a year. The Indian cobra feeds on rodents, lizards, other snakes, frogs  and small birds and their eggs (Daniel 2002, Whitaker and Captain 2004).
documentation.threats: This species is likely to be under localized pressure due to demand for venom collection and for the leather industry, despite bans on the legal collection of these snakes in India. Scores of individuals are collected, defanged and maintained by snake charmers for their livelihoods, but as this is a common and adaptable species this is unlikely to represent a major threat at a global scale. As venomous snakes that can be common in agricultural land, cobras are also subject to persecution.
documentation.measures: In India, this snake is protected by the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. It is present in many protected areas. It is an important agent of pest control, as a common snake that feeds on rodents in agricultural land. The venom of this species is used medicinally for its anticoagulant properties, and is being clinically tested for treatment of carcinomas. Genetic studies between the Indian and Sri Lankan populations are needed to determine if they may represent different species.
documentation.use_trade: Cobras are hunted and killed for their skins. The Government of India has, however, controlled the export of cobra skins since 1973. Nevertheless, a few tanneries deal with thousands of skins per day and continue to prosper. All members of the genus Naja are listed under CITES. Cobra venom is collected by captive farming of individuals for antivenom preparation. Illegal collection of cobras for venom extraction also occurs. Cobras are used as a means of livelihood by snake charmers in India.
documentation.rationale: Although the species is facing threats due to harvesting pressure, owing to its wide distribution, abundance and adaptability it is listed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Naja naja was described by Linnaeus in 1758 as Coluber naja basing on drawings by Seba (1734) from India (Smith 1943).
